column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: On the periodic table, what are the vertical columns called?
column28: Vertical columns are groups (older notes also call them families). Horizontal rows are periods.
column29: Vertical means up and down. Which word goes with up-and-down columns, and which goes with side-to-side rows?

column9: Which part of the periodic table indicates the number of energy levels in an atom's electron cloud?
column28: The period (horizontal row) tells the number of energy levels. The group (column, or family) tells the number of valence electrons.
column29: One location tells valence electrons and the other tells energy levels. Which one is the row?

column9: Elements in the same period have the same number of valence electrons.
column28: False. Elements in the same period (row) have the same number of energy levels. Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of valence electrons.
column29: Which tells valence electrons: the row or the column?

column9: The elements in Group 18, such as neon and argon, are called the ___.
column20: noble gases|noble gas|the noble gases|noble gasses
column28: Group 18 is the noble gases. They are nonreactive because they are already chemically stable.
column29: This group's name sounds like royalty, and its members are all gases.

column9: Lithium, sodium, and potassium are all in Group 1. What is the name of this group?
column28: Group 1 (not counting hydrogen) is the alkali metals. Alkaline earth metals are Group 2, halogens are Group 17, and noble gases are Group 18.
column29: Group 1 holds the most reactive metals. Which name goes with Group 2, so you can rule it out?

column9: Chlorine (Cl) is in Group 17. How many valence electrons does a chlorine atom have?
column28: For Groups 13–18, take off the 1 in front (skip the transition metals): Group 17 → 7 valence electrons.
column29: Groups 1 and 2 match their number. For Groups 13–18, use the last digit of the group number.

column9: Potassium (K) is in Group 1, Period 4. How many energy levels (shells) does a potassium atom have?
column28: The period number equals the number of energy levels. Period 4 → 4 energy levels.
column29: Which location tells energy levels: the group or the period?

column9: Where are the metals located on the periodic table?
column14: To the left of the staircase line
column15: To the right of the staircase line
column28: Metals are to the left of the metalloids (the staircase line). Nonmetals are to the right, except hydrogen, which sits on the left but is a nonmetal.
column29: Find the staircase line. Most elements are metals, so they take up the bigger side.

column9: Which of these are properties of metals? Select all that apply.
column15: Good conductor of heat and electricity
column28: Metals are shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable (can be hammered into sheets), and ductile (can be pulled into wires). Brittle and poor conductors describe nonmetals.
column29: Think of copper wire and aluminum foil. What can you do to them, and what do they carry?

column9: Helium is a noble gas, so it has 8 valence electrons like the rest of Group 18.
column28: False. Helium is the exception in Group 18: it has only 2 electrons total, so it has 2 valence electrons. Its one shell is full with 2.
column29: How many electrons does helium have in all? Can it have more valence electrons than that?

column9: Which of these elements is a metalloid?
column28: Boron is a metalloid. The metalloids sit along the staircase: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te. Carbon and sulfur are nonmetals; sodium is a metal.
column29: Metalloids touch the staircase line. Which choice is right next to it, at the top of the line?

column9: The elements in Group 17, such as fluorine and chlorine, are called the ___.
column28: Group 17 is the halogens, the most reactive nonmetals.
column29: This group holds the most reactive nonmetals. Its name means "salt-former."

column9: The modern periodic table organizes all the known elements by ___.
column16: the year each element was discovered
column28: The periodic table organizes all the elements known to exist by atomic number and chemical properties. Ordering by atomic mass was Mendeleev's first table; Moseley switched it to atomic number.
column29: What number goes up by exactly one from each box to the next?

column9: Hydrogen is in Group 1, but it is not an alkali metal.
column28: True. Hydrogen belongs with the group number (1 valence electron) but not with the group name. It is a nonmetal gas, so it is not an alkali metal.
column29: Is hydrogen a metal or a nonmetal?

column9: Match each group name to how it behaves.
column16: Noble gases :: Nonreactive; already chemically stable
column17: Alkaline earth metals :: Reactive metals with 2 valence electrons
column18: Transition metals :: Skipped when counting valence electrons
column28: Alkali metals are the most reactive metals. Halogens are the most reactive nonmetals. Noble gases are nonreactive because they are already chemically stable. Alkaline earth metals have 2 valence electrons. Transition metals (Groups 3–12) are skipped when counting valence electrons.
column29: Two names say "metals" and are reactive; one is the MOST reactive. Which group never reacts?

column9: Gallium (Ga) is in Group 13, Period 4. How many valence electrons does a gallium atom have?
column28: Skip the transition metals: Group 13 → 3 valence electrons. The period (4) tells energy levels, not valence electrons.
column29: For Groups 13–18, drop the 1 in front of the group number.

column9: Selenium (Se) is in Group 16, Period 4. How many valence electrons does a selenium atom have?
column28: Group 16 → 6 valence electrons (skip the transition metals in Groups 3–12). Period 4 would be the number of energy levels.
column29: Valence electrons come from the group, not the period. Then skip Groups 3–12.

column9: Strontium (Sr) is directly below calcium in Group 2. Calcium is in Period 4. How many energy levels does a strontium atom have?
column28: Directly below Period 4 is Period 5, and the period number equals the number of energy levels: 5.
column29: Moving down one box puts you in the next row. Which row is that?

column9: Nitrogen (N) is in Group 15, Period 2. How many valence electrons does a nitrogen atom have?
column28: Group 15 → 5 valence electrons. A common mistake is answering 2, which is the period (energy levels).
column29: Use the group, not the period. Drop the 1 in front of 15.

column9: Calcium (Ca) is in Group 2, Period 4. Which describes a calcium atom?
column28: Group 2 → 2 valence electrons. Period 4 → 4 energy levels. The other choices swap the group and period or use one number twice.
column29: The group gives valence electrons; the period gives energy levels.

column9: Why do elements in the same group have similar chemical properties?
column14: They have the same number of energy levels
column15: They have the same number of valence electrons
column16: They have the same atomic mass
column17: They have the same number of neutrons
column28: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, and valence electrons decide how an atom reacts. Same energy levels describes a period, not a group.
column29: Which electrons take part in reactions, and what does the group number tell you about them?

column9: Sodium (Group 1, Period 3), calcium (Group 2, Period 4), potassium (Group 1, Period 4), and chlorine (Group 17, Period 3). Which pair would have the most similar chemical properties?
column28: Sodium and potassium are both in Group 1, so both have 1 valence electron and behave alike. Being in the same period (like calcium and potassium, or sodium and chlorine) does not make elements behave alike.
column29: Look for the two elements that share a group, not a period.

column9: Boron, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen have atomic numbers 5, 6, 7, and 8, and each atom has 2 energy levels. They are all members of the same ___.
column28: Same number of energy levels means the same period (row): Period 2. They are in different groups because they have different numbers of valence electrons.
column29: Which location on the table tells the number of energy levels?

column9: Which of these elements are nonmetals? Select all that apply.
column28: Oxygen, sulfur, and neon are nonmetals (right of the staircase). Sodium and iron are metals, and silicon is a metalloid on the staircase.
column29: Nonmetals are right of the staircase line. Watch out for one element that sits ON the line.

column9: Where are the metalloids found on the periodic table?
column14: In Groups 3–12 in the middle of the table
column15: In Group 18 on the far right
column16: Along the staircase line between metals and nonmetals
column17: In the two rows below the main table
column28: The metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) sit along the stair-step (zig-zag) line between the metals on the left and the nonmetals on the right.
column29: Metalloids are "in between" metals and nonmetals. Where would an in-between group sit?

column9: For nonmetals, reactivity increases as you move down the group.
column28: False. For nonmetals, reactivity decreases as you move down the group. It is metals whose reactivity increases as you move down. That is why fluorine is the most reactive nonmetal.
column29: The most reactive nonmetal, fluorine, is at the top of its group. What does that tell you?

column9: Lithium (Period 2), sodium (Period 3), potassium (Period 4), and cesium (Period 6) are all in Group 1. Which one is the most reactive?
column28: For metals, reactivity increases as you move down the group. Cesium is lowest (Period 6), so it is the most reactive of these.
column29: Do metals get more or less reactive going down a group?

column9: Fluorine (Period 2), chlorine (Period 3), bromine (Period 4), and iodine (Period 5) are all in Group 17. Which one is the most reactive?
column28: For nonmetals, reactivity decreases as you move down the group, so the top one, fluorine, is the most reactive. Fluorine is the most reactive nonmetal on the table.
column29: Halogens are nonmetals. Do nonmetals get more or less reactive going down?

column9: Why do the noble gases not react in nature?
column15: They are already chemically stable with a full outer shell
column16: They are metals, and metals do not react
column17: They have the most protons of any group
column28: Noble gases are nonreactive because they are already chemically stable: their outer shell is full. They do have electrons, and they are nonmetals, not metals.
column29: What is special about a noble gas's outermost energy level?

column9: Sample X is a shiny gray solid, but it shatters when hit and conducts electricity only partway (a semi-conductor). Sample X is most likely a ___.
column28: Metalloids are solids with physical properties like metals (shiny) but are semi-conductors and can be brittle. A metal would bend, not shatter; a noble gas is not a solid.
column29: Shiny points one way, brittle points the other. Which class is in between?

column9: Which of these would be the best conductor of electricity?
column28: Silver is a metal, and metals are good conductors of heat and electricity. Iodine and argon are nonmetals (poor conductors), and silicon is a metalloid (only a semi-conductor).
column29: Decide which choice is a metal. Metals are the good conductors.

column9: Which of these would be the least reactive?
column28: Argon is a noble gas (Group 18), and noble gases are nonreactive because they are already chemically stable. Iodine is a halogen, a reactive nonmetal.
column29: Which choice is in Group 18?

column9: Hydrogen is not an alkali metal. So why is it placed in Group 1?
column15: It is a shiny, soft metal
column16: It has 1 energy level, like all Group 1 elements
column17: It is the most reactive metal
column28: Hydrogen has 1 valence electron, so it belongs with the group number. It does not belong with the group name, because it is a nonmetal gas, not a reactive metal.
column29: What does the group number tell you about an atom's electrons?

column9: Identify the element: I am the alkaline earth metal in Period 3. Type my name or symbol: ___
column28: Alkaline earth metals are Group 2. Group 2, Period 3 is magnesium (2 valence electrons, 3 energy levels).
column29: Which group number are the alkaline earth metals? Then go to the third row.

column9: When drawing a Bohr model from an element's spot on the periodic table, which step comes LAST?
column15: Fill electrons from the inside out (2, 8, 8)
column16: Check that the valence electrons match the group number
column28: The last step is a check: the electrons in the outer shell should match the group number (Groups 1, 2, 13–18). You can only check after the shells are filled.
column29: Which step looks back at the finished drawing?

column9: Identify the element: I am a Period 2 nonmetal with 6 valence electrons. Type my name or symbol: ___
column28: Period 2 → 2 energy levels. 6 valence electrons → Group 16. Group 16, Period 2 is oxygen.
column29: Turn 6 valence electrons into a group number (add 10). Then find that group in the second row.

column9: Identify the element: I have 6 energy levels and 8 valence electrons. Type my name or symbol: ___
column28: 6 energy levels → Period 6. 8 valence electrons → Group 18 (noble gas). Group 18, Period 6 is radon.
column29: Energy levels give the period. 8 valence electrons means the noble gas column.

column9: Identify the element: I am in the same group as bromine (Br), but I have fewer protons than magnesium (atomic number 12).
column28: Bromine is a halogen (Group 17). The only halogen with fewer than 12 protons is fluorine (atomic number 9). Neon has 10 protons but is a noble gas, not in bromine's group.
column29: First name bromine's group. Then check which choice in that group has an atomic number under 12.

column9: Identify the element: I have 3 valence electrons and 4 energy levels.
column28: 3 valence electrons → Group 13. 4 energy levels → Period 4. Gallium is in Group 13, Period 4. Aluminum and boron have 3 valence electrons but fewer energy levels.
column29: Change each clue into a location: valence electrons → group, energy levels → period.

column9: Period 3 contains Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, and Ar. Identify the element: I am the only metalloid in Period 3. Type my name or symbol: ___
column28: The metalloids are B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, and Te. Silicon is the only one in Period 3; aluminum is a metal and phosphorus is a nonmetal.
column29: Find where the staircase line crosses the third row.

column9: Identify the element: I am a metalloid, and my most common isotope has 70 neutrons. Most common isotopes (atomic number): Ge-74 (32), As-75 (33), Sb-121 (51), Te-130 (52).
column29: Subtract the atomic number from each mass number.

column9: Identify the element: I am a shiny solid that conducts electricity well and reacts violently with water. I have 5 energy levels.
column28: Shiny, conducts, and reacts violently with water → an alkali metal (Group 1). 5 energy levels → Period 5. That is rubidium. Potassium is an alkali metal but has only 4 energy levels.
column29: Which group name matches "shiny metal that reacts violently"? Then use the energy levels to pick the row.

column9: An element is in Period 3 and has 5 valence electrons. What is its atomic number?
column28: Period 3 → 3 shells. Fill from the inside out: 2 in the first, 8 in the second, 5 in the third (2-8-5). 2 + 8 + 5 = 15 electrons, so 15 protons: atomic number 15 (phosphorus).
column29: Draw the shells: how many shells for Period 3? Fill the inner ones, put the valence electrons on the outside, and add them up.

column9: Neon (Ne) is in Group 18, Period 2. How many valence electrons does a neon atom have?
column28: Group 18 → drop the 1 → 8 valence electrons. Neon has 10 electrons arranged 2-8, so its outer shell holds 8.
column29: For Groups 13–18, drop the 1 in front of the group number.

column9: An element is in Group 2, Period 4. Using shell capacities of 2, 8, 8, how many electrons does a neutral atom of this element have?
column28: Period 4 → 4 shells. Group 2 → 2 valence electrons in the 4th shell. Fill the inner shells: 2-8-8-2. 2 + 8 + 8 + 2 = 20 electrons (calcium).
column29: Fill the inner shells completely, then put the group's valence electrons in the outer shell. Add them up.

column9: An element is in Group 14, Period 3. Which electron arrangement does it have?
column28: Period 3 → 3 shells. Group 14 → 4 valence electrons. Fill from the inside out: 2-8-4 (silicon). 4-8-2 fills from the outside in, 2-4 has only 2 shells, and 2-8-8-4 has 4 shells.
column29: Count the shells from the period, put the valence electrons in the last shell, and fill inside out.

column9: An atom's electrons are arranged 2-8-7. Where is this element on the periodic table?
column28: 3 shells → Period 3. 7 valence electrons → Group 17 (skip the transition metals). Group 17, Period 3 is chlorine.
column29: The number of shells gives the period. The electrons in the last shell give the group (for 3 to 8 valence electrons, add 10).

column9: Jae says, "Iron (Fe) is in Group 8, so it has 8 valence electrons." Which response is best?
column14: He is right; valence electrons always equal the group number
column15: He is wrong; the valence rule skips the transition metals in Groups 3–12
column16: He is wrong; iron would have 18 valence electrons
column17: He is wrong; the period number tells valence electrons, not the group
column28: Jae is wrong. Groups 3–12 are transition metals, and the valence rule skips them. It only works for Groups 1, 2, and 13–18 (Group 18 = 8, except helium).
column29: Which groups does the valence electron rule work for?

column9: Sodium (Group 1, Period 3) and chlorine (Group 17, Period 3) have similar chemical properties because they are in the same period.
column28: False. Being in the same period only means the same number of energy levels. Sodium has 1 valence electron (reactive metal) and chlorine has 7 (reactive nonmetal), so they behave very differently.
column29: Similar properties come from having the same number of what? Do sodium and chlorine share that?

column9: Beryllium (atomic number 4), magnesium (12), strontium (38), and barium (56) are all in Group 2. Put them in order from least reactive to most reactive.
column28: Higher atomic number means lower in the group. For metals, reactivity increases as you move down the group: Be, Mg, Sr, Ba (least to most reactive).
column29: Use atomic number to decide which is lowest in the group. Do metals get more reactive going down?
